name: TMJ Botox

card.summary: Botulinum toxin injected into jaw muscles to ease temporomandibular disorders and bruxism; trials exist but results are mixed in the sources and it is off-label in most places.
card.aka: Botulinum toxin for TMD, masseter / lateral pterygoid Botox
card.note: Studied for jaw pain and disc problems, not as a proven appearance treatment; many registered trials are small or lack posted results.

quick.overview:
TMJ Botox refers to injecting botulinum toxin into jaw muscles, such as the masseter or lateral pterygoid, to calm overactive muscles in people with temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) or teeth grinding. It is a clinician-administered prescription treatment.

In looksmaxxing talk it is framed as a way to relax hyperactive jaw muscles. Wikipedia reports multiple randomized trials of lateral pterygoid injection with evidence of benefit, while a set of newer registered trials is still small and evolving.
quick.mechanism: Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at nerve endings, temporarily weakening the injected muscle. In TMD the rationale is that lateral pterygoid spasm may contribute to anterior disc displacement.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes that toxin spread can cause a fixed facial expression that resolves as the effect wears off. Effects typically last months. Use for TMD is generally off-label.

lead: TMJ Botox is the use of botulinum toxin injections in the jaw muscles to treat temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD), bruxism (clenching and grinding), and related jaw pain. It is performed by clinicians and is a prescription treatment.[1]

According to Wikipedia, injection into the lateral pterygoid muscle has been studied in multiple randomized trials with evidence of benefit, and effects typically last months. The theory behind the approach is that spasm of this muscle contributes to anterior disc displacement.[1]
Numerous trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, including small recently completed studies, but the registry entries reviewed here do not report outcomes.

paras: Investigators have registered trials of botulinum toxin for TMD with bruxism, anterior disc displacement, myofascial pain, TMJ dislocation and scleroderma-related restriction of mouth opening.[2][3][4][5][6][7][8]
Registered trials also compare toxin with other treatments, including arthrocentesis, splints, acupuncture and dry needling.[4][9][10][11]
Wikipedia's TMD article states that lateral pterygoid injection has been examined in multiple randomized trials with evidence of benefit.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov registrations include: a Phase 1 study of Botox for TMD with bruxism that was withdrawn (NCT02202070);[2] a completed 10-patient study of ultrasound-guided toxin injection for disc displacement with reduction (NCT07076355);[3] a completed 39-patient study combining i-PRF after arthrocentesis with lateral pterygoid Botox (NCT06207955);[5] a completed Phase 2/3 study of 20 patients with bilateral TMD (NCT05651256);[8] a completed 17-patient early-phase study in scleroderma (NCT04523506);[6] a randomized trial comparing arthrocentesis with toxin (NCT07736521) not yet recruiting;[4] and a 60-person study of splint, toxin, or medication plus splint care for clenching and jaw symptoms (NCT07586072).[11] Other registered studies compare a mandibular splint with toxin and compare acupuncture, dry needling and toxin.[9][10] Results are not posted in the registry entries.
No studies found on facial appearance outcomes of TMJ Botox.
A reported complication is a fixed facial expression from toxin diffusing to nearby muscles, which resolves as the effect wears off.[1]
The treatment is described in appearance-focused circles as a way to calm hyperactive jaw muscles. No published research tests it for facial appearance.
